references.text: The same law about returning a poor man's cloak before sunset, with the reasoning that it is his only blanket to sleep in
Prohibition against taking a widow's cloak as collateral, extending protection for the vulnerable
Job describes the wicked who take cloaks as collateral from the poor
Description of the poor lacking clothes and blankets, and those who take a widow's ox as collateral
The righteous returns what he has taken as collateral
Reiterates that the righteous returns collateral to the poor
Condemnation of those who lie on clothes taken as collateral at the altar
Continuation of the same text emphasizing God's gracious character
God's declaration of Himself as gracious and merciful
Confirms that the Lord is a merciful and gracious God
Both verses link God's ability to hear a cry directly to His nature as gracious, illuminating how grace is the foundation for answered prayer.
Psalm 91:15 is a direct allusion to Exodus 22:26's promise that God hears when one cries out in distress.
The verses form a theological contrast: the cry to the true God in Exodus is heard because of grace, while the cry to the idol in Isaiah reveals human delusion.
Both verses emphasize that God's grace is the decisive condition for Him hearing and answering a desperate cry.
Both verses highlight the necessity of God breaking His silence and hearing the cry of one standing in a vulnerable position.
Both verses confirm the theology that God turns His ear and answers when the believer cries out to Him.
Psalm 18:7 gives a concrete example of the fulfillment of Exodus 22:26's promise that God hears when one cries out in distress.
